source_text: ad hoc ista dixit Apostolus, ut sese cohiberent, qui asserebant laudi Dei proficere peccata mortalium, eumque ideo impossibilia praecepisse, ut miserendi sibi materiam praepararet: et per hanc apostolicam sententiam - sicut existimas - demonstratur, propterea recte iudicari homines, quia praecepta possibilia non fecerunt; iniuste autem iudicarentur, si ea non fecissent, quae impossibilia iuberentur
pass_a_gloss: To this that he-said apostle, so-that/as sese cohiberent, who asserebant laudi of-God proficere sins mortal, him-and for-that-reason impossible praecepisse, so-that/as miserendi to-himself materiam praepararet: and through this apostolicam position - as existimas - demonstratur, propterea rightly iudicari human-beings, because precepts possible not fecerunt; unjustly however iudicarentur, if she/it not fecissent, which impossible iuberentur.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: “And how will God judge the world? For if God’s truth has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?” (Romans 3:6–7)
By these words the apostle shows that God would have lost the authority to judge if he had not kept within proper bounds in commanding.

The apostle said this to restrain those who maintained that the sins of mortals increase God’s praise, and that he therefore commanded impossible things in order to provide himself with an occasion for mercy. This judgment of the apostle shows that human beings are rightly judged because they failed to do what was possible. They would be judged unjustly if they had failed to do things they were commanded to do but could not do.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
